passage:
Come here, Varun, sit. You asked how I found our first investors. I'm Sangeeta, and I'll tell you what I did, because I did it the slow way.
Everybody said, "Email everyone." I thought, no. First I made a list of sixty names: angel investors and small funds who had already backed health startups here. Then I ranked them in two columns: how well they fit us, and whether anyone I knew could introduce us. Dr Menon, my old professor, knew four of them and wrote two warm lines to each.
My co-founder and I kept it all in one shared sheet, and after every contact we wrote what happened. Nine of the top fifteen replied. Two of them met us. That was the start.

qa.q: How many of the top fifteen investors replied?
qa.a: Nine of the top fifteen replied.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta likely feeling when nine of the top fifteen replied?
qa.a: Sangeeta was likely relieved and quietly proud, since the slow ranking had paid off, though the passage gives this only as a mild hint in the 'That was the start.'

qa.q: Sangeeta chose to rank the names before sending anything. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It focused limited time on investors most likely to care and to open a message, instead of scattering emails to everyone.

qa.q: How might an investor who got a warm note from Dr Menon have seen the message?
qa.a: The investor would see it as coming from someone they trust, so it was more likely to be opened and read.

grounding: The elder's story shows a founder listing sixty investors, ranking them by fit and warm introductions and tracking each contact in a shared sheet.

Tushar had ten days before the demo day in Bengaluru, and in that time the power in his Bhopal neighbourhood cut out every afternoon. So he worked from 6 am to noon, on a charged laptop and a phone hotspot.
The job was the list. He read up on health-tech deals in India and noted every angel and seed fund that had backed one: sixty names by Wednesday. Then he ranked them. Did they invest at this stage? In clinics or diagnostics? Did anyone he knew know them? Shalini, his co-founder, went through her college contacts and found warm introductions to eleven.
By the weekend the shared sheet had columns for fit score, who could introduce them, date contacted and reply. The top twenty were in green. On demo day, when an investor asked, "Who else are you talking to?", Tushar could answer precisely.

qa.q: How many names were on the list by Wednesday?
How might Tushar have felt when the investor asked who else they were talking to?
qa.a: He probably felt confident and calm, since the sheet let him answer precisely.

qa.q: What else could make the list more useful after demo day?
qa.a: Updating replies after each meeting and moving investors up or down as they learn more about fit.

qa.q: How does Shalini's work change the list?
qa.a: Shalini's college contacts turned eleven cold names into warm introductions, making those investors more likely to reply.

grounding: It shows a founder listing sixty angels and seed funds that backed Indian health-tech, ranking them by fit and warm introductions and tracking each in a shared sheet.

subtype: Approach: building a target investor list [Action]
passage:
In their third-floor office in Hitech City, Yogesh pinned one rule above his desk: "No investor email without a row in the sheet." Over two weeks he built the list with Nazia, his co-founder: sixty investors, both angels and seed funds, who had backed health-tech startups in India, from a diagnostics investor in Pune to a doctor-angel in Chennai.
Each row got three scores: stage fit, sector fit and warmth, meaning how close anyone they knew was to that investor. Nazia called her old manager and got two introductions; Yogesh's professor offered three more. Cold names with low fit went to the bottom.
Every Friday at five they opened the sheet together and updated it: contacted, replied, meeting, follow-up. When a fund in Mumbai replied within an hour, Nazia grinned and moved its row to "meeting".

qa.q: What rule did Yogesh pin above his desk?
qa.a: "No investor email without a row in the sheet."

qa.q: What does Nazia's grin suggest she felt?
qa.a: Nazia felt pleased and encouraged that the careful ranking was paying off with a quick reply.

qa.q: Why does ranking by warmth matter?
qa.a: Investors are more likely to reply to an introduction from someone they know, so starting there saves time.

qa.q: What would change if Yogesh emailed all sixty on the same day without ranking?
qa.a: Low-fit investors would ignore them, and the warm introductions might be wasted or delayed.

grounding: It shows founders building a list of sixty health-tech angels and seed funds in India, scoring them by fit and warm introductions and tracking every contact in a shared sheet.
